prompt: A city bike-share scheme analyses its trip data. Name the type of analytics each question shows.

cases.text: How many trips started at each station last month?
Why did trips from the train station fall by half in March?
How many bikes will riders want at the beach stations next summer?
cases.explanation: Predictive: what might happen in the future?

cases.text: Which stations should the van restock first tomorrow morning?
cases.explanation: Prescriptive: what should we do next? It yields a recommendation for the next step.

cases.text: Which hour of the day had the most rentals this year?
cases.explanation: A summary of what already happened.

cases.text: Why do bikes at one station need repairs twice as often as the rest?
cases.explanation: It looks for the cause behind something that happened.

cases.text: What price for a day pass would bring in the most riders next season?
cases.explanation: It asks for the optimal course of action, not only a forecast.

prompt: A radio station plans to become a streaming audio app. Sort each challenge into technology or business.

cards.text: Servers that keep working when ten times the usual listeners tune in for a big match
cards.explanation: Infrastructure to support demand, like Netflix's cloud infrastructure.

cards.text: Compressing shows so they sound clear on a weak phone signal
cards.explanation: Encoding that keeps high fidelity yet stays lightweight.

cards.text: Moving from income from on-air adverts to paid monthly subscriptions
Other apps offering the same shows, and illegal copies shared online
Getting listeners to come back to the app every week
A player that streams on phones, cars and smart speakers
cards.explanation: A technical capability the service has to build.

prompt: A hospital moves from paper charts to electronic patient records. Put its change effort in the order of Kotter's eight steps.

steps.text: The director shows staff how lost paper charts led to repeated tests and delays.
steps.explanation: 1. Create a Sense of Urgency: the risks of not changing.

steps.text: Respected senior nurses, doctors and the IT lead form a group to lead the change.
steps.explanation: 2. Build a Guiding Coalition: influential people with authority, expertise and credibility.

steps.text: The group sets out a picture of every patient's record available on any ward in seconds.
steps.explanation: 3. Form a Strategic Vision and Initiatives: the desired outcomes.

steps.text: The vision is shared at every ward meeting and in the staff newsletter.
steps.explanation: 4. Communicate the Vision to all stakeholders.

steps.text: Staff get training, tablets and help on the wards to use the new system.
steps.explanation: 5. Empower Broad-Based Action: training, resources and support.

steps.text: The first ward to go paperless is celebrated for cutting waiting times.
On the strength of that success, the system is extended to pharmacy and outpatients.
steps.explanation: 7. Consolidate Gains and Produce More Change: larger change initiatives.

steps.text: Electronic records become part of hospital policy and of training for every new hire.
steps.explanation: 8. Anchor New Approaches in the Culture: policies, procedures and ongoing communication.

prompt: A bank's branch staff are moving to a new customer system. For each person, name the ADKAR outcome they have not yet reached.

cases.text: A clerk asks why the bank is replacing a system that works perfectly well.
cases.explanation: She does not yet understand the need for change or the reasons behind it.

cases.text: A teller knows why the change is coming but wants no part of it.
cases.explanation: He is aware of the change but does not want to support or participate in it.

cases.text: An adviser is keen to switch but has never been shown how the new screens work.
cases.explanation: He lacks the knowledge of how to change: training and resources.

cases.text: A cashier finished the training but still freezes when a real customer is waiting.
cases.explanation: Knowledge is not enough: she still has to practise the new skills and implement them.

cases.text: After a month with no recognition or support, a team quietly goes back to paper forms.
cases.explanation: Without reinforcement the change is not maintained over time.

cases.text: A manager fears the new system will be used to monitor her team, so she delays the switch.
cases.explanation: An unaddressed concern blocks the desire to support the change.

prompt: Two teams are each building a new mobile app for a gym chain. Sort what each team does into traditional or agile project management.

cards.text: Writes a 60-page specification of every screen before any work begins
cards.explanation: A fixed target defined upfront through detailed planning.

cards.text: Starts from one sentence: members should book a class in under a minute
cards.explanation: A flexible vision that serves as a guiding principle.

cards.text: Needs a sign-off form from the steering committee to add a new button
cards.explanation: Changes to the plan require formal processes and approvals.

cards.text: Releases a small piece every two weeks and asks members what to improve
cards.explanation: Small iterations, with feedback from stakeholders after each one.

cards.text: Judges success by finishing on the date and budget set at the start
cards.explanation: Success measured by adherence to the initial plan, timeline and budget.

cards.text: Drops a planned chat feature when members ask for workout tracking instead
cards.explanation: Adjusts to feedback even if the end goal shifts.

prompt: A small team builds an online shop for a bakery with Scrum. Match each principle of Scrum with what the team does.

pairs.match: The team checks real order data each week and changes its plan when checkout turns out to be the slow part.
pairs.explanation: Decisions based on what is known: transparency, inspection and adaptation.

pairs.match: The developers decide among themselves who builds the menu page and how.
pairs.explanation: Teams organize their work without being directed by outside authorities.

pairs.match: The baker joins the team every few weeks to try the shop and talk it through.
pairs.explanation: Teamwork and communication among team members, stakeholders and customers.

pairs.match: Online ordering is built before the recipe blog, because orders bring in money.
pairs.explanation: The most important features first, by the value they deliver.

pairs.match: Every planning meeting ends after one hour, whether or not the debate is finished.
pairs.explanation: A fixed time limit creates urgency and focus.

pairs.match: The shop goes live with one product page, then grows a little every two weeks.
pairs.explanation: Small, incremental cycles with regular feedback and adjustments.

prompt: A Scrum team builds a ticket app for a theatre. Sort each task to the role responsible for it.

cards.text: Puts seat selection at the top of the backlog after talking to theatre-goers
cards.explanation: The voice of the customer, managing the product backlog.

cards.text: Explains to the team what the theatre means by a group booking
cards.explanation: Ensures that the team understands the items in the backlog.

cards.text: Gets the payment provider to fix the test account that has blocked work for two days
cards.explanation: Removes impediments that hinder the team's progress.

cards.text: Asks the marketing director to stop sending the developers urgent side requests
cards.explanation: Shields the team from external distractions and interruptions.

cards.text: A designer, two developers and a tester build and test the seat map together
cards.explanation: A cross-functional group that delivers the product increment.

cards.text: Decides among themselves how to split the work on the checkout this sprint
cards.explanation: The development team self-organizes to decide how to do the work.

prompt: A team runs a two-week sprint on a food-delivery app. Put its events in order.

steps.text: The team picks the top backlog items and agrees the goal: pay with a saved card.
steps.explanation: Sprint Planning opens the sprint: what work will be done, and the sprint goal.

steps.text: On the first morning, each member says what they will do today in a 15-minute meeting.
steps.explanation: The Daily Scrum is held every day during the sprint.

steps.text: A week in, a developer says at the stand-up that the bank's test server is down.
steps.explanation: The Daily Scrum also surfaces impediments: what obstacles are in my way?

steps.text: On the last day the team shows the restaurant owners the working card payment.
steps.explanation: The Sprint Review demonstrates the completed work at the end of the sprint.

steps.text: Afterwards the team discusses what went well and what to change next sprint.
steps.explanation: The Sprint Retrospective is held after the review.

question_text: At the end of a sprint, a team has built a search bar that works but has not been tested, and a filter that is built and tested to the team's quality and acceptance criteria. What belongs in this sprint's increment?
hint: The increment must meet the team's definition of "done".
correct_answer_citation: Increment: The sum of all completed product backlog items at the end of a sprint. The increment must meet the team's definition of "done," which includes quality criteria and acceptance criteria.

options.option_explanation: Right. Only the filter meets the definition of "done", so only it is part of the increment.

options.option_text: Both the filter and the search bar
options.option_explanation: The search bar has not met the quality criteria, so it is not done and not part of the increment.

options.option_text: Neither: the increment is the list of work still to do
options.option_explanation: The list of work still to do is the product backlog. The increment is the completed work.

options.option_text: Everything the team selected for this sprint
options.option_explanation: That is the sprint backlog. The increment holds only the items that are completed and done.
